notes: Jockey Club penalty challenge; Richards J upheld five-year disqualification as proportionate on supervisory review.

enrichment.short_title: Bradley v Jockey Club: proportionality of disqualification for passing racing intelligence
key_facts: Former steeplechase jockey Graham Bradley admitted at a drugs trial that he had passed confidential horse information to professional gambler Brian Brendan Wright's organisation for rewards.
The Jockey Club found breaches of Rules 62(ii)(c) and 204(iv) and initially disqualified him for eight years; the Appeal Board reduced the penalty to five years.
Bradley challenged the disqualification as disproportionate, arguing comparable breaches had attracted only short bans and that weeks or months would suffice.
A five-year disqualification threatened to destroy his bloodstock agency business and seriously affect his livelihood and family.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Claim for review of a Jockey Club Appeal Board penalty decision; jurisdiction accepted though not by way of judicial review.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; the five-year disqualification was held a lawful and proportionate penalty within the Appeal Board's discretionary judgment.
enrichment.ratio: Although the Jockey Club is not amenable to judicial review, the court may supervise an Appeal Board penalty decision for proportionality; where serious breaches of integrity rules over many years warranted disqualification, a five-year ban was within the range of reasonable responses.
legal_issues: Whether review of the penalty rested on contractual or non-contractual supervisory jurisdiction
Whether the five-year disqualification was disproportionate compared with earlier Jockey Club penalties
Whether the Appeal Board properly assessed the seriousness of passing confidential racing information for reward
Whether the court should substitute its own view on the appropriate penalty period

notes: Section 40 GMC appeal; Collins J quashed SPM finding where care failures were below standard but not serious misconduct.

enrichment.short_title: Nandi v GMC: appeal against serious professional misconduct finding
key_facts: Dr Nandi, a GP in a deprived North London practice, was found guilty of serious professional misconduct by the GMC Professional Conduct Committee.

Allegations concerned technical temporary registration of a patient, inadequate telephone assessment of Mrs H before her later death, and failure properly to assess a schizophrenic patient Mr R after social services contact.
Dr Nandi was willing to accept practice conditions but contested the SPM finding; sanctions imposed were conditions on registration.
Collins J held the Committee's fact findings were not clearly wrong but the conduct, viewed in the round over a 30-year career, did not meet the serious professional misconduct threshold.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal under section 40 of the Medical Act 1983 against a GMC Professional Conduct Committee finding of serious professional misconduct.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; the SPM determination and associated sanction were quashed, with costs to Dr Nandi.
enrichment.ratio: Serious professional misconduct requires a serious falling short of standards expected among medical practitioners; conduct that merely falls below Good Medical Practice without being deplorable or seriously negligent does not suffice, and the court will interfere where the Committee has drawn the line too harshly.
legal_issues: Whether the Committee's fact findings were clearly wrong
Whether inadequate patient care over three incidents amounted to serious professional misconduct
Whether undertakings could replace an SPM finding
The proper deference owed to the Committee's expertise on professional standards

Ghosh v General Medical Council [2001] 1 WLR 1915
Evans v General Medical Council (Privy Council, unreported)

notes: Excise duty winding-up petition dismissed against respectable guarantor; DSMEG and Cipriani validity issues arguable.

enrichment.short_title: HMCE v Anglo Overseas: excise duty assessments and winding-up petition
key_facts: Anglo Overseas Ltd, a long-established logistics company, guaranteed duty-suspended whisky movements subcontracted to another carrier; falsified AADs showed delivery abroad but goods were diverted in a 'slaughter' fraud.
HM Customs assessed AOL to over £4.5 million excise duty and presented a winding-up petition despite AOL not being alleged complicit in the fraud and being solvent apart from the assessments.
AOL disputed liability under DSMEG regulation 4, argued Cipriani invalidated the four-month rule against innocent guarantors, and said part of later assessments was time-barred.
HMCE had participated in a VAT and Duties Tribunal appeal process before abruptly presenting the petition.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Companies Court hearing of a winding-up petition based on disputed excise duty assessments under DSMEG.
enrichment.outcome: Petition dismissed; AOL could dispute the debts on substantial grounds and winding up was an inappropriate debt-enforcement route for an innocent bystander guarantor.
enrichment.ratio: The Companies Court should not wind up a respectable solvent company on a genuinely disputed excise duty debt where the guarantor was not implicated in fraud, statutory interpretation issues remain arguable, and HMCE had acquiesced in tribunal proceedings.
legal_issues: Whether regulation 4 of DSMEG applied where goods did not arrive at the declared destination
Whether Article 20(3) and regulation 4 were invalid against an innocent guarantor after Cipriani
Whether part of the second tranche of assessments was out of time under section 12(4)
Whether presenting a winding-up petition was an abuse of process after tribunal participation

notes: High-profile ancillary relief appeal settled by mediation; lump sum and war chest set aside by consent.

enrichment.short_title: Al-Khatib v Masry: mediated settlement of international family finance appeal
key_facts: Mumby J ordered transfer of overseas properties worth about £13.5 million, a £10 million lump sum and a £2.5 million litigation 'war chest' after the husband abducted the children to Saudi Arabia in breach of wardship orders.
Limited permission to appeal was granted on the lump sum and war chest; the property transfer order was not appealed.
Court-directed mediation failed initially through administrative shortcomings, but resumed with experienced family and Muslim community mediators after an international arrest warrant crisis.
The parties reached Heads of Agreement reuniting the children with their mother and substantially reducing the husband's financial liabilities.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from ancillary relief and wardship-related financial orders, adjourned repeatedly for Court of Appeal mediation under judicial supervision.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed by consent; the £10 million lump sum, £2.5 million war chest, arrears and interest were deleted, with agreed child contact and divorce arrangements including a lawful talaq.
enrichment.ratio: Even highly conflicted cross-border family appeals may be resolved through properly supervised appellate mediation with appropriately skilled mediators and active judicial oversight of process crises.
legal_issues: Whether Mumby J's financial awards were excessive given Middle Eastern family context
Whether the husband's contempt precluded appellate review
How appellate mediation should be administered in complex family cases
Enforceability of overseas property transfer and litigation funding orders
linked_authorities: Hadkinson v Hadkinson [1952] P 285
Al-Khatib v Masry [2002] 1 FLR 1053

confidence.notes: Consent outcome limits ratio on merits, but procedural mediation guidance is clear.

notes: Renewed asylum permission refused; adjudicator's post-evidence torture questioning held fair.

enrichment.short_title: Ates v SSHD: fair hearing and adjudicator questioning in fast-track asylum appeal
key_facts: Turkish appellant claimed he was tortured for three days in March 2004 before arriving in the UK on 12 April 2004.
The adjudicator questioned him after cross-examination about the severity of falaka torture and concluded the account was fabricated because injuries were inconsistent with the alleged treatment.
The Immigration Appeal Tribunal held an independent observer would regard the hearing as fair and that the adjudicator was clarifying severity to assess lack of medical evidence.
Maurice Kay LJ had refused permission on paper; Brooke LJ dismissed the renewed application.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed application for permission to appeal against an Immigration Appeal Tribunal decision dismissing a fast-track asylum appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Application for permission to appeal dismissed; no arguable error of law in the IAT's fair-hearing assessment.
enrichment.ratio: An adjudicator may ask questions after re-examination to clarify evidence and assess credibility, including persistence on the severity of alleged torture, provided the questioning is not hostile and the tribunal correctly applies the fair-hearing test.
legal_issues: Whether the adjudicator's questioning gave rise to apparent bias or an unfair hearing
Whether repeated questions about falaka amounted to a dogged pursuit of the issue
Whether lack of medical evidence could support rejection of torture claims
Whether the IAT erred in applying the independent observer fair-hearing test
linked_authorities: Koller v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2001] EWCA Civ 1267
Oyono v Secretary of State for the Home Department (IAT, unreported)

confidence.notes: Procedural fairness issue and dismissal are clearly reasoned.

notes: Commercial Court preliminary issues on construction liability insurance; global settlement did not ascertain insured loss.

enrichment.short_title: Lumbermens v Bovis: insured loss ascertainment after Braehead settlement

statutes_considered.title: Supply of Goods and Services Act 1982

key_facts: Bovis settled Technology and Construction Court litigation over the Braehead retail centre for £15 million without apportioning Braehead's £103 million counterclaim for mismanagement and defects.
Bovis claimed about £19.2 million from Lumbermens under construction professional liability policies based on its solicitors' subjective assessment of valid counterclaim elements.
The insurers sought negative declarations that no indemnity was due because liability and loss had not been ascertained by judgment, award or settlement.
Colman J tried four preliminary issues on ascertainment, subjective loss measurement, insuring clause construction and warranty disclosure.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Commercial Court trial of preliminary issues in insurers' claim for declarations of no liability under primary and excess liability policies.
enrichment.outcome: Issues 1 and 2 answered No: the global settlement did not ascertain insured loss and extrinsic subjective or objective allocation could not supply it; issue 3(a) No and 3(b) partly yes; issue 4(b) No for undeclared warranty cover under clause 2.
enrichment.ratio: Under a liability policy there is an implied term that the assured's loss must be specifically ascertained by judgment, arbitration award or settlement; a global compromise without identifying the cost of discharging insured liabilities does not trigger indemnity even if the assured can prove underlying liability.
legal_issues: Whether Bovis's liability was ascertained by the £15 million global settlement
Whether insured loss could be measured by Bovis's subjective contemporaneous assessment
Whether insuring clause 1 required proof of negligence or covered non-negligent error or omission
Whether breach of clause 2.5.2.5 warranty cover required annual contract declaration under memorandum 7(i)

notes: Recognition evidence in small community; Clarke and Baker followed; no ID parade but conviction safe.

enrichment.short_title: R v Williams: recognition evidence and community reputation names
key_facts: Andrew Williams appealed against conviction for inflicting grievous bodily harm on Martin Francis on the Taff Trail in August 2003.
Witness Michael Summers recognised the assailants as Andrew and Paul Williams, brothers known in Upper Abercanaid, though he had learned their names from others over many years.
No identification parade was held despite defence request; the recorder applied R v Clarke and Baker on community recognition.
Williams did not give evidence and relied on alibi and a no-case-to-answer submission based on hearsay identification.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with leave against conviction in the Crown Court at Merthyr Tydfil.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the conviction was safe despite breach of the identification parade Code, which was addressed in summing-up.
enrichment.ratio: Repeated community identification of locally known persons may support recognition evidence rather than inadmissible hearsay where the witness had seen the defendants often over years; Clarke and Baker applies and differs from the single-sighting facts in R v Fergus.
legal_issues: Whether Summers' evidence of the assailants' identity was inadmissible hearsay
Whether the case was one of recognition rather than dock identification
Whether failure to hold an identification parade rendered the conviction unsafe
Whether Clarke and Baker was correctly applied and should be followed
linked_authorities: R v Clarke and Baker [2003] EWCA Crim 718
R v Fergus [1992] Crim LR 363
R v Turnbull [1977] QB 224

notes: 1957 outline permission construed as all-purpose access; PSV-only condition quashed on appeal.

enrichment.short_title: Redrow v Secretary of State: traffic use conditions on 1957 planning access
key_facts: Outline planning permission granted in 1957 permitted construction of three accesses to existing public highways for a large Gloucestershire industrial development, including access at point 6C to the B4055.
Condition 6 expressly restricted goods traffic at point 6B, but condition 5 only reserved approval of location and detailed construction plans.
In 2003 the Secretary of State approved detailed plans but imposed a condition limiting access at 6C to public service vehicles only because of changed motorway traffic conditions.
Sullivan J quashed the condition as an impermissible modification of the 1957 permission; the Secretary of State appealed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal under section 288 of the 1990 Act against quashing of reserved-matter approval conditions on a historic outline permission.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed with costs; the 2003 PSV-only condition unlawfully derogated from the all-purpose access granted in 1957.
enrichment.ratio: Where a 1957 permission granted access to an existing all-traffic public highway without express restriction, condition 5 did not permit later imposition of a class-of-traffic limitation; contrast with condition 6 showed restrictions had to be expressly stated.
legal_issues: Whether the 1957 permission was for an all-purpose or restricted access at point 6C
Whether condition 5 allowed traffic-class restrictions when approving detailed construction plans
Whether changed highway conditions since 1957 could justify modifying the permission via reserved matters
Whether condition 6 rendered condition 5's silence on traffic use otiose

R v Ashford Borough Council, ex p Shepway District Council [1988] PLCR 12
Probern Developments Ltd v Secretary of State [1990] 3 PLR 79

notes: First reported s67 Sexual Offences Act 2003 voyeurism sentence appeal; eight months replaced by CRO.

enrichment.short_title: R v IP: first voyeurism sentence appeal under section 67 of the 2003 Act
key_facts: The appellant installed a video camera in a loft above the bathroom to observe his 24-year-old stepdaughter showering for sexual gratification.
He pleaded guilty to voyeurism under section 67(1) and installing equipment under section 67(4) after the family discovered the linked bedroom screen.
The Crown Court sentenced him to eight months' imprisonment concurrent on each count.
There was no circulation of recordings; the appellant was of previous good character with early guilty pleas and left the family home.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with leave against sentence in one of the first cases under section 67 of the Sexual Offences Act 2003.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; imprisonment replaced by a one-year community rehabilitation order with participation in a Community Sex Offender Group Work Programme; notification period reduced to five years.
enrichment.ratio: Even serious intra-family voyeurism involving covert recording may not require immediate custody where the offender is of good character, pleaded early, did not distribute images, and probation recommended rehabilitation.
legal_issues: Whether eight months' imprisonment was manifestly excessive for section 67 voyeurism
Appropriate sentence for first-offender covert filming of an adult stepdaughter
Whether a community rehabilitation order with sex offender programme was sufficient
Consequential effect on Sex Offenders Act 1997 notification period

notes: Chapman v Simon applied; EAT restored dismissal where race complaint not pleaded.

enrichment.short_title: Akinmolasire v NHS Trust: unpleaded race discrimination complaint
key_facts: Justinah Akinmolasire, a black Nigerian employee of Camden and Islington Mental Health NHS Trust, was dismissed after an extended probation review in October 2001.
The employment tribunal upheld one complaint that the employer failed to investigate her race discrimination allegation made at the end of the probation meeting and awarded £2,240.
The originating application and interlocutory documents did not specifically plead failure to investigate a complaint made on 22 October 2001.
The Employment Appeal Tribunal allowed the employer's appeal applying Chapman v Simon; the Court of Appeal dismissed the employee's appeal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against an Employment Appeal Tribunal decision reversing a race discrimination finding in favour of the claimant.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the tribunal's finding on the unpleaded October 2001 investigation failure could not stand and no remittal was warranted.
enrichment.ratio: An employment tribunal may find unlawful discrimination only in respect of acts specifically complained of; a discrete finding on failure to investigate an allegation made at a probation meeting cannot be supported where that act was not pleaded.
legal_issues: Whether paragraph 44 of the tribunal reasons related only to the 22 October 2001 complaint or earlier events
Whether the failure to investigate was a continuing act or just and equitable to extend time
Application of Chapman v Simon to limits of tribunal jurisdiction
Whether the whole case should be remitted to a fresh tribunal

linked_authorities: Chapman v Simon [1994] IRLR 124
